elements.id-string-2: \title{On-Device Evaluation Toolkit for Machine Learning  on Heterogeneous Low-Power System-on-Chip}
elements.id-string-3: \author{Zhaolan Huang, Koen Zandberg, Kaspar Schleiser and Emmanuel Baccelli\thanks{Corresponding Author: Z.
elements.id-string-8: Schleiser are affiliated with Freie Universität Berlin.
elements.id-string-10: Baccelli is affiliated with Inria, France.

elements.id-string-15: Network delays, throughput bottlenecks and privacy issues push Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) designers towards evaluating the feasibility of moving model training and execution (inference) as near as possible to the terminals.
elements.id-string-16: Meanwhile,Results from the TinyML community demonstrate that, in some cases, it is possible to execute model inference directly on the terminals themselves, even if these are small microcontroller-based devices.
elements.id-string-17: However, to date, researchers and practitioners in the domain lack convenient all-in-one toolkits to help them evaluate the feasibility of moving execution of arbitrary models to arbitrary low-power IoT hardware.
elements.id-string-18: To this effect, we present in this paper U-TOE, a universal toolkit we designed to facilitate the task of AIoT designers and researchers, by combining functionalities from a low-power embedded OS, a generic model transpiler and compiler, an integrated performance measurement module, and an open-access remote IoT testbed.
elements.id-string-19: We provide an open source implementation of U-TOE and we demonstrate its use to experimentally evaluate the performance of a wide variety of models, on a wide variety of low-power boards, based on popular microcontroller architectures (ARM Cortex-M and RISC-V).
elements.id-string-20: U-TOE thus allows easily reproducible and customisable comparative evaluation experiments in this domain, on a wide variety of IoT hardware all-at-once.
elements.id-string-21: The availability of a toolkit such as U-TOE is desirable to accelerate the field of AIoT, towards fully exploiting the potential of edge computing.
elements.id-string-23: AI, IoT, Low-power, Microcontroller, Toolkit, Benchmarks.
elements.id-string-25: As Artificial Intelligence (AI) permeates our lives more and more, mechanisms such as deep neural networks~\cite{sze2017dnn} are put to use (or their deployment planned) in more and more places in various distributed systems.
elements.id-string-26: The data pipeline with AI typically requires the creation and the use of a \emph{model}, i.e. a layered structure of complex algorithms (also known as \emph{operators}) which interpret data and make decisions based on that data.
elements.id-string-27: This model must first be trained, before it can be put to use in production~\cite{sze2017dnn}.
elements.id-string-28: Designing a distributed system combining AI and Internet of Things (AIoT) thus requires placing somewhere along the terminal-edge-cloud continuum both model training (learning) and model execution (inference).
elements.id-string-29: Recent work on TinyML~\cite{sanchez2020tinyml,ray2022tinyml-review} forays into optimizing models to fit tinier resource budgets (and to perform efficiently nevertheless) on low-power microcontrollers.
elements.id-string-30: As a consequence, both learning placement possibilities, and inference placement possibilities are extended to encompass ultra low-power terminals.
elements.id-string-31: However, generic and convenient open source tools lack for AIoT designers, who are required to:
elements.id-string-33: evaluate the performance of their models when placed somewhere along the terminal-edge-cloud continuum, especially when including potential placement on different microcontroller-based devices;fine-tune their models, and identifying performance bottlenecks at model layer granularity, on different microcontrollers;select an adequate microcontroller to execute their model, for a targeted task running on a low-power device to-be-designed.
elements.id-string-34: This paper thus introduces U-TOE, an open source AIoT toolkit which tightly combines a generic model compiler and a popular low-power IoT operating system to automatically compress, flash and evaluate arbitrary models (output of TensorFlow, PyTorch...) on arbitrary COTS low-power boards (such as BBC:microbit, nrf52840dk, Arduino Zero, HiFive...) based on the popular microcontroller architectures (ARM Cortex-M, RISC-V).
elements.id-string-35: {\bf Paper contributions.} Our contributions are given as follows:
elements.id-string-36: We designed a universal TinyML on-board evaluation toolkit for AIoT (U-TOE).
elements.id-string-37: It provides feasibility check of the deployment of arbitrary model on a given IoT hardware platform, allows researchers and developers to locate the performance bottleneck of a given model on target device.
elements.id-string-38: The evaluation results enable co-design with other components on system level, help optimizing ML models and configurations for specific use cases, allowing to achieve the best possible performance on target devices.We released the source code\footnote{see \url{https://github.com/zhaolanhuang/u-toe}} of U-TOE under an open licence.
elements.id-string-39: This implementation enables compilation, flashing, and evaluation of neural network (computational graph based) models from mainstream ML framework onto various low-power boards based on popular ISA.We provided benchmarks and a comparative experimental evaluation using U-TOE, reproducible on an open-access IoT testbed and on personal workstation, which both provides insights on inference performance with different models on different low-power hardware anddemonstrates how U-TOE can be re-used by TinyML experimental researchers and developers to fine-tune AIoT configurations.
elements.id-string-41: Recent work has surveyed \cite{saha2022tinyml-review} the scope of ML frameworks, tasks, metrics, including a comprehensive review on TinyML stack and deployment pipeline.
elements.id-string-42: A number of challenges need to be met in order to fit the tiny resource budgets typical of microcontrollers (kiloBytes of memory, power consumption in mWatt, CPU frequency in MHz) while maintaining performance at an acceptable level and retaining portability to extremely polymorphic hardware in this category.
elements.id-string-44: Various open source IoT operating systems are used to provide hardware abstraction, and resource sharing primitives as well as convenient peripheral access (e.g. sensor/actuator, network subsystem) on heterogeneous low-power microcontrollers.
elements.id-string-45: Prior work such as \cite{hahm2015operating} surveys such operating systems, among which prominent examples include RIOT\cite{baccelli2018riot} and Zephyr\cite{zephyr}.
elements.id-string-46: However, such software platforms so far offer very limited support for ML frameworks -- if at all.
elements.id-string-47: Moreover, the most advanced support so far are typically hardware- or vendor-specific e.g. with libraries provided by STM Cube or ARM CMSIS-NN.
elements.id-string-49: Various testbeds offer remote access to fleets of reprogramable microcontroller-based devices.
elements.id-string-50: Prior work such as \cite{lima2019testbeds,mitton2011testbeds} survey such testbeds, among which prominent examples include the open access facility IoT-lab \cite{adjih2015iot-lab}, which offers remote bare-metal access (serial over TCP) to a fleet composed of hundreds of popular low-power boards of various kind.
elements.id-string-52: Benchmarking ML on low-power hardware entails a number of challenges \cite{banbury2020benchmarking}.
elements.id-string-53: Prior work such as MLPerf Tiny \cite{banbury2021mlperf} provides a standard benchmark suite (a fixed set of representative ML tasks) for evaluating the performance of given hardware, and an online platform for manufacturers to publish their comparative benchmark results.
elements.id-string-54: In contrast, U-TOE offers a more powerful and more customizable toolkit for performing feasibilitys check of user-defined machines learning models on low-power devices, with a greater degree of flexibility and customization.
elements.id-string-56: Prior work such as \cite{osman2022tinyml-bench} focuses on performance comparison of different machine learning frameworks on two COTS low-power boards (Arduino Nano BLE 33 and STM32 NUCLEO-F401RE).
elements.id-string-57: In particular, it benchmarked two TinyML frameworks, TFLM and X-CUBE-AI over gesture recognition and wake word spotting.
elements.id-string-58: Other work such as \cite{sudharsan2021tinyml-bench} tested TFLM models on several microcontroller-based boards.
elements.id-string-59: While such papers provide a performance comparison of specific frameworks on specific boards for specific tasks, U-TOE offers greater flexibility and generality, allowing developers to evaluate a wider range of (user-specified) models on a larger variety of low-power devices, and to dive into the execution details of ML models.
elements.id-string-61: Compilers such as TVM \cite{chen2018tvm} can be used to automate the transpilation and compilation of models provided by major ML frameworks (TFML, Pytorch etc.) so as to expose low-level routines and optimize them for execution on specific processing unit characteristics (CPU, GPU etc.).
elements.id-string-62: An extension of TVM called uTVM was recently introduced, adding smaller hardware targets including a variety of MCUs (microcontroller units).
elements.id-string-64: ML-EXray\cite{qiu2022ml-xray} enables TinyML developers to gain visibility into the layer-level details of ML execution and diagnose cloud-to-edge deployment issues.
elements.id-string-65: Developers can analyze and debug edge deployment pipelines with high usability, using less than 15 lines of code for fully examination.
elements.id-string-66: However, the reliance on Tensorflow Lite restricts the capability to accommodate models from further ML frameworks and deploy on low-power devices.
elements.id-string-67: Major ML frameworks (TFML, Pytorch and MXNet etc.) provide internal profiler.
elements.id-string-68: Such tools allows developers to measure the performance of their models.
elements.id-string-69: They can be used to collect metrics such as inference time and memory usage, which can then be analyzed to optimize the model's performance.
elements.id-string-70: Though it can provide us execution details in layer level, it still lacks the supports for on-device deployment and evaluation on various IoT devices, while U-TOE is a more general-purpose toolkit that provides a comprehensive solution on a wide range of low-power devices.
elements.id-string-72: One the one hand, as the most immediate limiting resource budget on microcontrollers concern memory limitations, typically in the order of kiloBytes, TinyML performance evaluation typically focuses primarily on metrics measuring memory consumption -- while keeping an eye on execution speed -- as described below.
elements.id-string-73: On the other hand, TinyML performance analysis can be tackled at different granularity levels: at the global model level, or at the operator level, for finer granularity, as described in the following.
elements.id-string-75: The considered metrics offer insights into the feasibility, efficiency and resource utilization of offloading model inference burden to low-power devices.
elements.id-string-76: By analyzing these metrics, users can make initial decisions regarding model  selection, optimization techniques, and hardware configurations to maximize performance and minimize the resource footprint on low-power devices.
elements.id-string-78: This metric measures the amount of dynamic memory space (primary RAM) consumed by the model during inference.
elements.id-string-79: It reflects the memory footprint of the model activation and is important for low-power devices that have limited memory resources.
elements.id-string-80: Efficient memory utilization allows for the deployment of larger and more complex models on such devices.
elements.id-string-82: This metric quantifies the amount of storage space, typically in terms of Flash memory region, required to store the compute instruction and associated parameters.
elements.id-string-83: It reflects the model's storage footprint on the low-power device.
elements.id-string-84: Minimizing storage consumption allows for accommodating multiple models on the device or orchestrating with other essential applications.
elements.id-string-86: This metric measures the time consumption  of performing inference for each input sample, either at the model level or at the level of individual operators within the model.
elements.id-string-87: It reflects the inference speed of the model on the low-power device and plays crucial role in real-time or latency-sensitive applications.
elements.id-string-88: Core clock frequency, cache strategies and communication latency between memory and working core have great impact on this indicator.
elements.id-string-90: This metric considers the cost of the System-on-a-Chip (SoC) used in the low-power device.
elements.id-string-91: The price of the SoC affects the overall affordability and feasibility of deploying model in large-scale distributed system.
elements.id-string-92: Lower-cost SoCs can make the deployment more accessible and cost-effective.
elements.id-string-94: As for performance analysis of machine learning in other domains, TinyML performance can be measured at different granularity levels:
elements.id-string-96: At this coarse level, one measures performance of the model as a whole, i.e. the resource footprint incurred by the execution of the model including all its layers and operators.
elements.id-string-97: For example, this allows for evaluating the resource consumption for inference with the production-ready code, on a particular industrial hardware setup.
elements.id-string-98: This approach measures the resource footprint at model level.
elements.id-string-99: It uses the model code generated by AoT executor of uTVM, which is the production version for deployment and allows for simulation of the resource consumption of inference in industrial fields.
elements.id-string-100: With user-specific random inputs (uniform distribution by default), user can simulate various data scenarios.
elements.id-string-101: By measuring the model-level resource footprint, U-TOE provides insights into the IoT system co-design with other software components.
elements.id-string-103: At this level, one measures separately the performance of one or more operators (i.e. one or more components of the model).
elements.id-string-104: This per-operator measurement can help identifying specific operators that contribute to performance or inefficiencies, in optimizing the model's efficiency and spotting potential bottlenecks.
elements.id-string-105: U-TOE facilitates the evaluation of computational latency and memory usage for each operator within the model.
elements.id-string-106: This evaluation is achieved by leveraging the Remote Procedure Call (RPC) functionality provided by uTVM.
elements.id-string-107: U-TOE can then collect performance data for individual operators within the model.
elements.id-string-108: Additionally, U-TOE annotates relevant parameters (layer weights and bias etc.) associated with each operator, which enables further profiling and analysis.
elements.id-string-109: This per-operator measurement allows users to identify specific operators that contribute to performance or inefficiencies, aiding in optimizing the model's efficiency and identifying potential bottlenecks.
elements.id-string-110: Useful Background on RIOT, uTVM and IoT-Lab
elements.id-string-111: U-TOE combines the use of RIOT as general-purpose embedded software platform, uTVM as transpiler/compiler of models, and IoT-Lab as open access IoT hardware testbed.
elements.id-string-112: Hence, we provide below some additional background on these building blocks.
elements.id-string-118: U-TOE integrates uTVM and RIOT to perform model compilation, flashing, and evaluation of arbitrary models from mainstream ML frameworks onto various COTS low-power boards.
elements.id-string-119: The toolkit is composed of the following key components:
elements.id-string-121: U-TOE leverages the uTVM compiler to convert arbitrary neural network models into efficient C code.
elements.id-string-122: This compiler enhances the efficiency of the models and enables them to be run on low-power devices.RPC Mechanism.
elements.id-string-123: To evaluate the resource consumption at operator level, U-TOE utilizes the Remote Procedure Call (RPC) mechanism of uTVM.
elements.id-string-124: The RPC mechanism enables to upload and launch functions on to IoT boards over serial.
elements.id-string-125: This is useful for remote testing and profiling, enabling U-TOE to wrap the model operators for measuring the computational latency and memory usage.
elements.id-string-126: It is composed of a client on the host and a server on the target device, receiving commands and executable instructions from the host.OS Environment.
elements.id-string-127: RIOT was chosen to provide a lightweight runtime environment for model execution and evaluation on microcontrollers, with its advantages in extensibility and wide-spectrum support for low-power boards.Evaluation Module.
elements.id-string-128: It contains two units: measurement worker and analyser.
elements.id-string-129: As shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:utoe-sw-setup}, the measurement worker is deployed on the MCU for acquiring performance metrics at model or operator level.
elements.id-string-130: Besides carrying out the measurement of resource footprint, It is in charge of the randomization of model input, and responsible to report metrics data to host device.
elements.id-string-131: The analyser runs on the host, statisticizes the uploaded metrics from device and provides human-readable frontend for users.
elements.id-string-132: Additionally, U-TOE provides a \emph{connector} for cloud-based IoT testbed which enables seamless interaction with remote boards using serial over TCP.
elements.id-string-133: As depicted in Fig.~\ref{fig:utoe-hw-setup}, users can evaluate and benchmark their models on local device, or on a remote, scalable testbed with wide-range of MCUs via U-TOE connector.
elements.id-string-139: {\bf Compilation and Deployment --} U-TOE first gathers the specification of target device to decide the compilation options for uTVM and RIOT.
elements.id-string-140: Then, as presented in Fig. \ref{fig:utoe-compile-and-deploy}, uTVM generates sub-optimal model library of the input model without scheduling\footnote{A schedule specifies low-level optimization for loop execution, enhancing cache hit and memory access.
elements.id-string-141: The optimal one is co-determined by model and device specification, and identified by heuristic search algorithms based on measurements on device.
elements.id-string-143: Some static optimization strategies are applied in this stage according to target device type.
elements.id-string-144: This uTVM-generated library is jointly compiled with RIOT, RPC server and measurement worker into executable firmware, which is then automatically flashed on the device.
elements.id-string-145: {\bf Evaluation --} After deploying the program on the target device, a bidirectional channel -- in Per-Operator evaluation --, or a unidirectional channel -- in Per-Model evaluation -- is set up between host and device, as depicted in Fig.~\ref{fig:utoe-sw-setup}.
elements.id-string-146: The measurement worker starts collecting performance metrics at user-specified level and uploads metrics data to analyser.
elements.id-string-147: Eventually, users can obtain the overall statistics of model metrics, or catch the performance bottleneck with execution details of each operator.
elements.id-string-148: All the raw metrics data are saved in log file for further, user-customized analysis.
elements.id-string-150: We designed two measurement procedures to support evaluation at different granularity.
elements.id-string-151: The procedures run across multiple components of the toolkit and the most workloads are primary on the target board.

elements.id-string-181: We conducted experiments to validate the functionality and compatibility of U-TOE on model side (universal support for model structure and ML frameworks) and on device side (wide-spectrum support for IoT devices).
elements.id-string-182: Hence, we dived into two orthogonal directions: For device support, we evaluated a quantized LetNet-5 on various IoT boards; For model compatibility, we evaluated multiple models on a local STM32F746G discovery board.
elements.id-string-183: \textbf{Model Selection} We selected pre-trained, quantized models from open source repositories\footnote{see \url{https://github.com/ARM-software/ML-zoo} and \url{https://github.com/mlcommons/tiny}}, which target on typical TinyML tasks (Image Classification, Key Word Spotting, Visual Word Wake, Noise Suppression and Abnormal Detection).
elements.id-string-184: The weights and activations of the model were quantized to 8-bit integer, yet the inputs and outputs remain in IEEE FP32 format.\textbf{Model Optimization} We only used built-in, rule-based optimization in uTVM.
elements.id-string-185: Thus, all heuristic optimization strategies like model scheduling were disabled.\textbf{MCU Configuration} We disabled data and instruction cache to observe the "memory wall" effect in ML model.
elements.id-string-186: The core clock frequency was pre-set by CPU initialization code in RIOT and is presented with experiment results in Section ~\ref{sec:results}.\textbf{Hybrid Deployment} The experiments were conducted both on local and remote IoT boards provided by FIT-IoT Lab.
elements.id-string-187: It is noted that for each evaluation we preset the number of trials to ten in order to address random error.

elements.id-string-223: On the one hand, researchers and practitioners who possess IoT hardware that is supported by the open source operating system RIOT (currently 250+ types of boards, using 60+ types of CPUs~\footnote{see \url{https://github.com/RIOT-OS/RIOT/tree/master/boards}} can use U-TOE out-of-the-box, directly on their boards.
elements.id-string-224: On the other hand, combined with the use of the free open-access testbed IoT-Lab~\footnote{see \url{https://www.iot-lab.info/}}, even researchers and practitioners who do not have such hardware on premises can conduct large scale experimental comparative evaluation campaigns using U-TOE.
elements.id-string-225: {\bf Perspectives --} As RIOT board and CPU support expands and improves over time, and as uTVM also expands support to other architectures in parallel (both open source communities are very active) U-TOE can in a very short time expand its support for new use cases, automatically adding the support of uTVM for new boards, and the support of RIOT for new models.
elements.id-string-226: As such U-TOE may oragnically grow and become a useful link between the two communities.
elements.id-string-227: Moreover, while the work on U-TOE in this paper has been focused on inference only on single-core microcontrollers, there is strong potential to extend the toolkit provided by U-TOE to support on-device learning scenarios, and for optimizing exploitation of multi-core microcontrollers.

elements.id-string-232: In this paper we presented U-TOE, a novel toolkit we designed to substantially facilitate the task of AIoT practitioners, by enabling universal TinML model evaluation.
elements.id-string-233: Using U-TOE, the output of arbitrary machine learning frameworks can be evaluated on arbitrary low-power hardware based on different microcontroller architectures, all at once.
elements.id-string-234: The wide availability of such a toolkit is indeed desirable to accelerate the field of AIoT.
elements.id-string-235: We thus provided a highly re-usable, documented and customisable open source implementation of U-TOE, jointly harnessing the active open source communities around RIOT and uTVM.
elements.id-string-236: Finally, we also demonstrate the use of U-TOE, by providing initial experimental evaluation results on a wide variety of popular low-power boards used in the TinyML community, for a wide variety of models from a popular model zoo.

elements.id-string-252: Results from the TinyML community demonstrate that, it is possible to execute machine learning models directly on the terminals themselves, even if these are small microcontroller-based devices.
elements.id-string-253: However, to date, practitioners in the domain lack convenient all-in-one toolkits to help them evaluate the feasibility of executing arbitrary models on arbitrary low-power IoT hardware.
elements.id-string-254: To this effect, we present in this paper U-TOE, a universal toolkit we designed to facilitate the task of IoT designers and researchers, by combining functionalities from a low-power embedded OS, a generic model transpiler and compiler, an integrated performance measurement module, and an open-access remote IoT testbed.
elements.id-string-255: We provide an open source implementation of U-TOE and we demonstrate its use to experimentally evaluate the performance of various models, on a wide variety of low-power IoT boards, based on popular microcontroller architectures.
elements.id-string-256: U-TOE allows easily reproducible and customizable comparative evaluation experiments on a wide variety of IoT hardware all-at-once.

elements.id-string-266: {\bf Paper contributions.} Our contributions are as follows:
elements.id-string-267: We design a universal toolkit for TinyML on-board evaluation (U-TOE).
elements.id-string-268: It provides feasibility checks for the deployment of arbitrary model on a given IoT hardware platform.
elements.id-string-269: It allows researchers and developers to locate the performance bottleneck of a given model on a target device.
elements.id-string-270: The evaluation results enable co-design with other components at system level, help optimizing ML models and configurations for specific use cases, allowing to achieve the best possible performance on target devices.We released the code\footnote{see \url{https://github.com/zhaolanhuang/U-TOE/}} of U-TOE under an open source licence.
